rows.evidence: Q1: Methodology and Results sections <U+2013> the authors develop the WEBSOM algorithm (NSGA-II coupled with EPANET) and run it on the Palos de la Frontera network (227 hydrants, 3 pumping stations), reporting their own model runs (Tables 1-3, Figs 5-6).
rows.notes: The study does exactly what the passage describes: after k-means sectoring, a customized NSGA-II establishes a monthly pumping/sector calendar minimising energy consumption plus irrigation deficit (F1) and pressure failures plus pressure-deficit magnitude (F2). However, all results on supply reliability (zero irrigation deficit from generation 2 onward; 1-7 hydrants below 30 m service pressure) come from EPANET simulations run on design data (hydrant base demand = design flow 1.2 l/s/ha x area, all hydrants in a sector assumed open, pump efficiency assumed 0.8). The hydraulic model output is never checked against observed pressures or flows, although a telemetry system is mentioned. The only comparison with real data is the current measured energy consumption (4115 MWh) used as a baseline for the 20-29% savings figure, which is a scenario comparison rather than a validation and does not concern the pressure-failure/irrigation-deficit (risk-management) effect. Under the rule that unvalidated model runs on design data do not count, Q2 is answered no; a lenient reader could treat the method description as self-evidently supported. The paper also notes that the fully supplied-demand scenario is an upper bound and that actual water availability is usually lower, so pressures in practice would be higher; no dispersion measures or validation errors are reported.

notes: Full text available (post-print). Figures partly rendered as text; equations missing from the extraction but described in prose. Study is a model/optimization paper applied to a real district; no field validation of simulated pressures reported.
